A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same Brownian-bridge encoder and evaluation metric. Their text, equations, figures, tables, and complete appendices are readable and support comparison, including matching renamed and relocated content.

before.justification: V1 reports original coherence-discrimination, GCDC human-rated coherence, cross-dataset transfer, and HC3 human–AI comparison results, together with encoder analyses.

after.justification: V3 retains original empirical results and reports additional classifier, WSJ transfer, baseline-comparison, and latent-representation analyses in the main text and appendices.

M1.justification: The BB Encoder becomes the SP Encoder and the proposed BBScore becomes SPM without changing their core architecture, likelihood objective, covariance updates, or score formula. V3 adds the SPM+CLS variant, which feeds whole-trajectory and moving-window scores into a task-specific perceptron (Section 4.1; Appendix C).

E1.justification: V3 removes GCDC evaluation across Enron, Clinton, Yahoo, and Yelp, eliminating the human-rated coherence task. It adds WSJ news articles for transfer evaluation while retaining WikiSection, WikiText, and HC3. The Mixed Shuffle test corresponds to v1's existing article-wise relative-score comparison.

E2.justification: V3 adds DetectGPT and heuristic BBScore to HC3 comparisons, Entity Grid and heuristic BBScore to mixed-shuffle comparisons, and Unified Coherence and BBScore to transfer comparisons. Removing GCDC also removes its Lai–Tetreault SOTA and readability-baseline comparisons. The original global/local WikiSection comparator set remains.

E3.justification: V1 Section 5.2 reports training on WikiText and testing on WikiSection; v3 Section 4.3 and Table 5 report the reverse direction despite retaining the same eight SPM test scores. This establishes a reported protocol revision, not confirmed rerunning. V3 also introduces WSJ splits and length filtering, and DetectGPT evaluations with 1 versus 10 perturbations.

E4.justification: V3 adds score-versus-article-length analysis, covariance and latent-deviation diagnostics, per-dimension trajectory examples, and a WikiSection/WikiText overlap audit (Figure 2; Appendices D–F). Appendix G adds DetectGPT perturbation-budget sensitivity. V1's aggregate latent-trajectory comparison and regularization exploration are retained.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or significance tests for performance estimates. V3's new latent-deviation boxplots describe representation variability rather than uncertainty over experimental runs; the covariance-estimation method remains unchanged.

E6.justification: V3 adds SPM+CLS results, including 97.42% and 97.36% global accuracy at block sizes 5 and 10, plus WSJ and additional baseline results. DetectGPT reaches 64.30%/63.30% with one perturbation and 84.89%/83.13% with ten. Original SPM HC3 scores remain 70.67%/69.71%. GCDC results and training-set score columns disappear; the relabeled transfer scores do not demonstrate a new performance gain.

T1.justification: The Brownian-bridge likelihood, covariance MLE, normalized chi-square score, and Appendix A proofs remain mathematically equivalent. Theorems become propositions or a definition. V3's concentration-near-one remark explains a property of the already derived normalized chi-square score rather than introducing a new theoretical result.

C1.justification: The central encoder and coherence-metric contributions remain. V3 adds a comparative claim about AI-detection performance at similar inference budgets, and its abstract asserts encoder superiority over contrastive learning without v1's explicit out-of-domain emphasis. Renaming the existing article-wise comparison as Mixed Shuffle does not itself introduce a new contribution.

C2.justification: V3 explains weak local discrimination through the whole-trajectory likelihood and develops covariance-based interpretations of detection and transfer results. It adds the limitation that DetectGPT performs better with more perturbations and an overlap-based justification for domain separation. V1's explicit caveats about heuristic hyperparameter selection and insufficient multi-domain/encoder evidence are removed.

D1.justification: V3 documents SPM+CLS window sizes and classifier widths, identifies a 32-dimensional latent example, specifies the overlap-matching procedure, and explicitly identifies WikiSection training for HC3 evaluation. Appendix B retains the original hardware, training durations, optimizers, learning rates, regularization settings, and submitted-code configuration reference.

R1.justification: V3 adds stochastic-interpolant context through two Albergo works, DetectGPT positioning, and Joty and WSJ citations; Krumm and Lim references disappear. The central relationship to Wang's contrastive encoder and Sheng's BBScore remains, with more explicit criticism of the latter's theoretical grounding and length sensitivity.

P1.justification: V3 extensively rewrites the abstract, introduction, method explanations, results narrative, and conclusion. It introduces contribution bullets and three organizing experimental questions, moves related work after results, reorganizes task presentation, and consistently distinguishes SP Encoder/SPM from the earlier BBScore baseline.

P2.justification: V3 redraws and relocates the framework diagram, merges global/local tables, and replaces the encoder-comparison bar chart with tables. It relocates and expands the latent-trajectory figure, adds covariance, moving-window, and article-length displays, and moves the original HC3 covariance-comparison table to Appendix G alongside new comparison tables.

improvement.justification: V3 improves exposition and adds useful diagnostics and baseline comparisons at different inference budgets. It also removes GCDC's human-rated coherence validation, while Table 5 reverses the training/test domains attached to the identical eight SPM scores in v1 Table 4 without explanation. The unresolved provenance of this central transfer evidence, together with the validation loss, prevents a reliable net-quality judgment.
